AI Foundations · Final project · October 2026

Bridge

A multi-agent app that helps long-distance couples stay close between calls.

AuthorSaya Sivaram
Codegithub.com/sayasivaram/bridge (the same link submitted on Canvas)
AppRuns locally from the repo in about two minutes (README: clone, venv, install, .env one folder up, seed, run)

In one sentence: Bridge turns the small moments two partners drop into a shared jar during the week into specific conversation starters for their next call, notices when the couple starts to drift, and suggests a ritual to do together tonight, while keeping each partner's private notes private.

2. Motivation

Why I built this. I moved away from my partner to attend Yale for two years, and so did several of my classmates. Between recruiting, classes, clubs, and everything else, it is easy for a relationship to take the back seat. My partner also travels abroad for months at a time (right now, Europe for the next six weeks), and we found ourselves simply connecting less. This is my life partner, and I don't want to come out of these two years with a weaker relationship. So I wanted a tool that helps us stay connected and still fits into both of our crazy schedules.

Couples who live apart, such as grad students like us, early-career professionals, people waiting on a visa, or military families, keep a relationship going mostly through scheduled calls. Those calls have a known failure mode: they open with "how was your day?", slide into logistics (flights, schedules, who calls when), and end before anything that actually happened that week comes up. The funny thing on the train, the song stuck in your head, the small win at work: by the time of the call they're forgotten, or they feel too small to bring up.

The second problem is slower. Distance hides drift. Partners in the same city notice when the other is quieter than usual; partners five time zones apart often don't, until it surfaces as a fight. In the demo couple's own words (seed data, written to mirror this pattern): Priya's week-3 check-in note says "Calls felt rushed this week. We mostly talked logistics." Leo's private note the same week says "Felt far away this week. Missed our Sunday cook." Neither knows the other felt it.

How people deal with it today: a running notes app or a starred-messages folder of "things to tell them", daily-question apps that ask both partners the same generic question, a shared calendar, or pasting texts into ChatGPT and asking for ideas. Each covers a piece. None of them uses what this couple actually lived this week, and none notices drift.

Why anyone should care: calls are the relationship for these couples, and making them better is cheap. Bridge costs about $0.0108 per couple per month to run (section 5), so it could be offered free.

Sources (checked October 22, 2026): paired.com and Paired's article on how answers are revealed; Lasting on the App Store and ChoosingTherapy's review; Couply on the App Store; Love Nudge on the App Store and in marriage.com's roundup; Pairy (its App Store listing has since been removed); Amora on Product Hunt; CoupleSpace on mwm.ai.

What Bridge does that these don't. Each piece exists somewhere: journals, daily questions, AI coaches. What is new is putting them together around the call, and doing it safely:

  • Grounded in the couple's real week. Starters come only from moments the couple logged, and code checks that every one cites a real, shared moment. A generic question app can't say "I need the full story about the cat in the backpack at your lecture."
  • Privacy between partners is a feature, not a setting. Each moment and note is shared or private. Private items never reach the other partner or any prompt whose output the other partner sees. Scores are revealed only after both have checked in, so neither anchors on the other.
  • Drift detection that is cheap and honest. Plain rules (score trends, a gap between partners, fewer moments, missed check-ins) run for free every week. The model is called only when they flag something, and then only to write one gentle, specific suggestion, never a diagnosis.

Honest limits of the claim: I didn't use every app in the table myself, and their features change. And it isn't one of the course's overdone ideas: not a chatbot over documents, a planner, a summarizer, or a study buddy. The LLM writes from this couple's own data, under rules checked in code.

4. The agents

Bridge has three agents and a router, all calling gpt-6-luna through one wrapper (app/llm.py). Every page button calls its agent directly; the Ask Bridge chat box goes through an orchestrator that checks the input, routes it, runs the agent, and checks the output.

ComponentRuns whenCan use (its tools)ReturnsChecked in code
Call-Topic Agent"Prep for our call", or the chatShared moments from the last 7 days; couple profile (names, time zones, inside jokes, shared stressors)5 starters + 1 deeper question, each citing moment idsIds must be shared moments in the window; no private text; 1 retry
Drift DetectorPulse page, or the chatLayer 1 rules (no model): 4-week signals. Layer 2 agent: those signals, shared notes, ritual ratingsOne suggestion + a short explanationCoach-boundary phrases, numbers must come from the signals; 1 retry, then a rule-based nudge
Ritual BuilderRituals page, or the chatCatalog of 25 rituals (filtered to tonight's time and energy in code); highest- and lowest-rated past rituals with notes3 catalog rituals: why, first step, optional twistIds in the catalog and fitting tonight; no invented bookings or purchases; 1 retry, then rule picks
RouterChat messages onlyKeyword rules first; an LLM classifier only on a tie or no matchOne of the three agents, or "ask the user"Strict enum; anything else asks the user

How they're organized. It's a hub, not a chain: agents don't call each other. The orchestrator owns one request context, so the router and agent share a request id, a step limit (6 calls), and one token total. Each agent validates its own output in code and gets at most one retry; the guard then checks the output again (schema and coach boundary) before anything is shown. Rules do the work wherever rules are enough: routing clear messages, detecting drift, filtering the ritual catalog, and screening for crisis language all cost nothing.

Model. gpt-6-luna through Portkey is the only model allowed on the course key, so every agent uses it, with strict JSON-schema output so answers can be validated. I set reasoning effort to "low" after measuring it (section 5): it cut the Call-Topic Agent's cost by 61% and its latency in half, and kept the quality gains of the better prompt.

One real run, step by step

Priya types "What should we do tonight?" into the chat. The trace below is the app's own log of that request (agent_runs), shown under the answer:

  1. Guard in: 26 characters, no injection pattern, no crisis language. It passes.
  2. Router: keyword rules score Ritual Builder 3 ("what should we do", "tonight") and everything else 0. A clear winner, so no model call: $0.
  3. Ritual Builder: code filters the catalog to the 20 rituals that fit about an hour at medium energy (the router read neither from the message, so it says what it assumed). It sends the couple's history: highest rated, a co-watch and the pasta cook-along (both 5.0/5); lowest, Codenames Duet (2.5/5, "too much strategy after a long work day").
  4. Model call: 2,950 tokens in (2,463 read from the prompt cache), 244 out, $0.00021. It returns three picks, each with why it fits, a first step, and an optional twist.
  5. Validation: all three ids are in the catalog and fit tonight, there are no bookings or purchases, and the ratings it cites (5/5) match the history. 3 of 3 pass.
  6. Guard out: the output matches its schema and has no coach-boundary phrases.
  7. Logged with the trace, tokens, and cost; the badge shows the total.

5. Tokenomics

Every model call is logged with its input, cached-input, cache-write, output, and reasoning tokens and its cost (llm_calls), and the app shows them: a badge on every answer and a Usage page. The numbers below are real runs, measured with python scripts/cost_report.py --measure 4 on fresh seed data (18 calls: four rounds of every agent plus four chat messages, two of which the router sent on to an agent, so those two agents have 5 runs; Portkey's response cache skipped so every call reached the model). Cost per user, and at scale

Assumptions, per user per week: call prep before two calls, ritual ideas twice, one Pulse nudge per couple (so half per user, because both partners share it), and one chat message the keyword rules can't route. They're editable at the top of scripts/cost_report.py.

Assumption, per userRuns / weekCost / runPer month

Expected cost: $0.00542 per user per month, about $0.0108 per couple. The hard ceiling is what a user would cost if they hit the 50,000-token daily budget every day, with every token at the most expensive rate: $0.7500 per user per month. The budget makes that ceiling a guarantee, not an estimate: a request that could go over is refused before the model is called (section 6).

What I did to keep cost down

  1. Prompt layout for caching. Every agent sends the stable part first (rules, the ritual catalog, the couple profile, byte-identical between runs and between partners) and the variable part last. 89% of all input tokens were read from the cache. For a call prep, input costs about $0.00003 instead of $0.00027. (Homework 6 measured that uncached input on this deployment is billed as cache writes at $0.125.)
  2. Reasoning effort "low". Default (medium) reasoning used 1,576 reasoning tokens per call-prep run in v2; low used 320. Cost per run went from $0.00107 to $0.00042, and latency from 16 s to 8 s.
  3. Rules before models. Clear chat messages are routed by keywords ($0). The Drift Detector's rules run for free and the model is called only on drift, so a quiet week costs nothing. The ritual catalog is filtered to tonight's time and energy in code, so the model only chooses.
  4. Never pay twice. A nudge is cached per couple and signals, so both partners share one call. Portkey also answers repeated identical requests from its own cache. llm.py reads Portkey's x-portkey-cache-status header, so those hits cost $0 and don't use up the budget, instead of being counted at full price.
  5. Budget and caps. A per-user daily token budget, a step limit of 6 calls per request, a cap on output tokens per call, and at most one retry per agent.

Did cutting cost make it worse? The evidence

I evaluated the Call-Topic Agent's prompt in three versions, 5 real runs each, with automated checks plus my own reading of every output (scripts/eval_call_topics.py, results in docs/evals/):

Call-Topic Agent, 5 runs eachv1 baselinev2 better promptv3 = v2 + low reasoning
Mean cost per run$0.00065$0.00107$0.00042
Mean latency16.7 s16.1 s8.0 s
Reasoning tokens per run7341,576320
Starters that just retell their moment (6+ words copied)14 / 250 / 250 / 25
Openers copying the prompt's example0 / 255 / 250 / 25
Empty answers (whole output cap spent on reasoning)010
Starters about Leo in Priya's runs3 / 156 / 155 / 15

The better prompt (v2) fixed the quality problems but cost 65% more, because the model thought much longer, and once it spent its whole output cap on reasoning and returned nothing (the retry recovered it). Lowering reasoning effort (v3) brought cost below the original with the quality gains intact. The one place v3 looks slightly worse is balance: one of three Priya runs had only one starter about Leo, against the rule's two. With 5 runs per version, that difference is within run-to-run noise; the large effects (retelling 14 → 0, cost, latency) are not.

6. Safety

The risks that matter for an app that holds two people's private feelings about each other:

RiskWhat I builtEvidence
Prompt injection in a moment, a note, or the chatUser text is HTML-escaped and wrapped in data tags; every system prompt says tag contents are data, never instructions. Chat messages are screened before routing.Demo cases 1–2; tests/test_prompt_injection.py, test_call_topics.py
A partner reading the other's private moments or notesThe privacy rule lives inside every SQL query in moments.py and pulses.py, and a test fails if any other code queries those tables. Prompts for one partner never select the other's private items.Demo case 3; test_moments_privacy.py, test_pulse.py
Invented factsEach agent's output is checked in code: cited moments must exist and be shared, ritual ids must be in the catalog, numbers and ratings must come from the data.Demo case 4; agent tests
The coach overstepping: diagnosing, predicting, taking sides, "you should break up"Boundary-phrase checks on every agent's output (retry, then a safe rule-based answer); "should we break up?" gets a gentle referral to a counselor before any model runs.Demo case 7; test_orchestrator.py, test_safety.py
Abuse, fear, self-harm, serious distressA keyword pre-check runs before any coaching, on private notes too. The author gets real helplines for their country (988 and the National DV Hotline in the US; Samaritans and the National Domestic Abuse Helpline in the UK). The other partner sees an ordinary quiet week, because they may be the person the author is afraid of. Flagged text never goes to a model.Demo case 5; test_pulse.py
Overspending and runaway loopsPer-user daily token budget checked before every call; step limit of 6 per request; output cap; one retry.Demo case 6; test_llm.py

Defenses shown working. python scripts/run_safety_demo.py runs seven attacks against the real app code. By default the model is scripted to act compromised, so it tries to do whatever each attack asks; this shows the code-side checks catching it even when the model misbehaves. All seven are defended. With --live, the real gpt-6-luna ignored both injections and gave safe answers on its own (3 cases, $0.00057).

Do the tests really test something? For each defense, I deleted it in a throwaway copy of the code and ran its tests: removing the privacy condition from the SQL fails 7 tests; removing the pulse reveal rule (enforced twice, in SQL and again in Python) fails 1; turning off the crisis pre-check fails 14; turning off the coach-boundary check fails 9; turning off the catalog check fails 3. In total there are 125 test functions (167 cases with their parameters): 166 run offline and spend no tokens, and one optional live check is skipped unless you turn it on.

7. Impact

What Bridge changes, with the numbers I can stand behind:

  • Prep goes from effort to seconds. Instead of scrolling back through a week of texts before a call, a partner presses one button and gets five specific starters in a median of 6.4 s, each linked to the moment it came from.
  • Specific, not generic. On the final prompt, 0 of 25 starters just retold a moment and none was generic ("how was your week?"); every one cited a real shared moment (automated checks, 5 real runs).
  • Something that wasn't possible before: noticing drift privately. The rules caught the demo couple's pattern (Leo's score 4 → 3 → 2, his shared moments 6 → 3 → 1, both saying contact was too little) and suggested one concrete fix, without revealing either partner's private notes to the other.
  • Cheap enough to be free: about $0.0108 per couple per month, and at most $1.50 even in the worst case. A nonprofit or university counseling center could offer it free: 1,000 students would cost about $5.42 a month at the measured rate.

What they told me: they said they would use Bridge, because adding a moment to the jar and doing the Pulse check-in each took very little effort. They liked how easy it was to move between tabs. Their one concern was the connection trend lines on the Pulse page: seeing their scores plotted over time might make them self-conscious about the relationship. Their suggestions are in section 8.

Limits of this test: one session, with the demo couple's data rather than their own.

8. Limits and next steps

What doesn't work yet:

  • No real accounts. "Viewing as" is a demo switch, so anyone running the app can view as either partner. The privacy rules hold for each viewer, but real logins are needed before real couples use it.
  • The crisis check is keyword-based. It is instant and testable, and it avoids common figures of speech ("this deadline is killing me"), but it will miss things a careful reader would catch and can misfire. Its card says so.
  • The page buttons skip the chat's output guard. Each agent checks its own output, but only chat requests get the second, uniform check.
  • Small evaluations. 5 runs per prompt version is enough to see large effects, not small ones. Starter quality was judged by automated checks and by me, not by couples.
  • Portkey's response cache returns the same answer to an identical request: free, but "Prep" twice with no new moments gives the same starters.
  • Tested on Python 3.14 on macOS; Python 3.11 and Windows are supported by the code and dependencies but untested.

What the tester asked for:

  1. Calendar integration. Add a planned ritual to both partners' calendars as a block, or let an agent read their availability (with permission) and suggest when to do it. The calendar would serve the ritual, not turn Bridge into a scheduler.
  2. Ask Bridge as a relationship coach. Offer reassurance and summaries, such as "what emotions did I report this week?", the question it couldn't answer in the test. The coach boundary would stay: no diagnosing, no relationship decisions, and the crisis check first.
  3. Custom rituals. Let couples add their own rituals to the catalog the agent picks from, checked the same way as the built-in 25 (time, energy, no purchases or bookings).
  4. A gentler view of the trend. Make the connection chart optional, or show a softer summary instead of plotted scores, so a dip doesn't make a couple feel watched.

With another month:

  1. A real pilot with 5–10 long-distance couples for three weeks, measuring how many starters they use per call and how their weekly Pulse scores move.
  2. Accounts and an invite flow: one partner invites the other; both can export or delete their data.
  3. Time-zone-aware reminders an hour before a call, with that call's starters ready, and a nudge to drop a moment when the jar has been quiet for days.
  4. A second safety layer: an LLM classifier behind the keyword pre-check, tested on a labeled set of notes, and the output guard on every path, not just the chat.
  5. Learning per couple: let ratings of starters ("we used this one") feed the Call-Topic Agent the way ritual ratings already feed the Ritual Builder.

How this report was made: every number comes from files in the repo and can be reproduced with scripts/cost_report.py, scripts/eval_call_topics.py --compare baseline v2 v3, and scripts/run_safety_demo.py. The report was drafted with an AI assistant and checked against the code.
